Coincident means "occupying the same point in time or space." When two things are coincident, they line up — either they happen at the same moment, exist at the same location, or match each other in some meaningful way.

Think of it as two separate things landing on exactly the same spot — whether that spot is a moment in time, a position in space, or a point of agreement.

1. Happening at the same time

This is the most common meaning. Two events are coincident when they occur during the same period or at the same moment.

"The economic crisis was coincident with the drought — both hit the country in the same year."

"The power cut was coincident with the start of the match."

Notice: it simply states they happened together. It doesn't say why or whether it was surprising. That's important (more on this below).

2. Occupying the same position in space (especially in geometry)

In mathematics and geometry, two lines, points, or shapes are coincident when they lie exactly on top of each other — they share every single point.

Imagine drawing a line on paper, then drawing another line directly over it so perfectly that you can't tell them apart. Those two lines are coincident — they are not just parallel, they are identical in position.

"When you solve a system of two linear equations and both equations turn out to be the same line, the lines are coincident — they have infinitely many solutions."

This meaning is precise and technical, but it follows the same logic: two things occupying the exact same spot.

3. In agreement or correspondence with something

Two things are coincident when they align, match, or correspond — when one fits neatly with the other.

"Her ambitions were coincident with the organization's goals — she was a natural fit."

"His observations were coincident with what the data showed."

Here, "coincident" means the two things are in harmony, pointing in the same direction.

In real usage, "coincident with" is the most natural construction. The word rarely stands alone without a "with" following it.

✅ "The launch was coincident with the anniversary of the company."
✅ "The flooding was coincident with the high tide."
✅ "His rise to power was coincident with a period of public unrest."

This is where most learners go wrong, so pay close attention.

These two words look related, and they are — but they carry very different meanings.

Coincidental means something happened by chance — it was unexpected, surprising, or accidental. It carries the sense of "what a strange accident!"

"It was coincidental that we both showed up wearing the same shirt — neither of us planned it."

Coincident is neutral. It simply states that two things happened at the same time or in the same place. It says nothing about whether this was surprising, planned, or accidental.

"The two meetings were coincident — they were both scheduled for 3 p.m." (Just a fact. No judgment.)

The test: Ask yourself — does the sentence need to imply chance or surprise? If yes, use coincidental. If you're just stating a neutral fact about timing, position, or correspondence, use coincident.
Register and where you'll encounter it

Coincident is a formal word. You will rarely hear it in casual everyday conversation. Instead, you'll encounter it in:

  • Academic writing ("The peak in crime rates was coincident with the period of unemployment.")
  • Scientific and research papers ("The rise in temperature was coincident with increased solar activity.")
  • Formal reports and journalism ("The policy change was coincident with the minister's resignation.")
  • Mathematics and geometry textbooks ("The two planes are coincident.")

In casual speech, people tend to say "at the same time," "overlapping," or "matching" rather than "coincident." So if you use this word, you're signaling a formal, precise register.
Putting it all together — varied examples

• "The blackout was coincident with the heavy storm — both occurred within the same hour." (timing)
  • "In the solution, the two equations yield coincident lines, meaning any point on one satisfies the other." (geometry)
  • "The CEO's resignation was coincident with the board's announcement of a new strategy." (timing, formal context)
  • "Her research findings were largely coincident with the earlier study published in 2019." (correspondence/agreement)
  • "The festival falls on a date coincident with the harvest season." (timing)

Coincident = two things landing on the exact same spot — in time, in space, or in meaning. No surprise implied, no accident assumed. Just alignment.

Once you have that image — two things landing precisely on the same point — all three meanings click naturally into place.
